81cf31d9e0.why: Old idiom fixed: all four choices say 'a bigger or smaller part' and stay parallel; the stem's 'half circle' is gone, so no stem word is echoed only by the key; the context no longer spells out 86175ed485's answer. Key true (NASA: 'The Sun always illuminates half of the Moon ... how much we are able to see of that illuminated half changes as the Moon travels through its orbit'). Lures are the sourced misconceptions (Earth's shadow, other planets' shadows, the Sun lighting more or less) and truly wrong; Earth's shadow reaches the Moon only in a lunar eclipse. 'Over about four weeks' fits the 29.5-day cycle. Core 6th-grade fact.

c2fedcf73b.why: Old polish done: the east and west horizons are cut, and the key is no longer the longest choice ('It goes all the way round Earth each day' is). Key true (NASA: 'A full Moon rises around sunset and sets around sunrise'; 'The Moon is opposite the Sun, as viewed from Earth'). Lures false and live: between Earth and the Sun is the new moon; most full moons are not at perigee; the Moon takes 27.3 days to go round Earth, and its daily rising comes from Earth's spin. The rise-at-sunset picture still points at opposite sides, but that is the grade's simple why, as the judge said. Context true.

6fd6deac45.why: Old tell fixed: the 'dims the daytime sky' clause is cut, so the night-side lure is live again (students picture a dark new moon on the night side). Key true (NASA: 'Solar eclipses only occur during the new moon, when the Moon and Sun are aligned on the same side of Earth'). Lures false: Earth between Sun and Moon, and the Moon in Earth's shadow, are the lunar eclipse; at new moon the Moon is in the daytime sky. Choices fully parallel ('Only then is...'). Named 6th-grade eclipse fact. Context true.

b260626b6b.why: Old dead lure fixed: 'Sunlight bounced off the other planets' is live (students know planets shine by reflected sunlight) and false: Venus at its brightest is about magnitude -4.6 and the full Moon -12.6, more than a thousand times apart, so planet light is far too faint, and it is not red. Old clarity fixed: 'What light makes it glow red?' has one answer. Key true (Grokipedia: 'Sunlight grazing the Earth's limb is bent toward the Moon by atmospheric refraction', blue scattered away, as at sunset). Earth's side facing the eclipsed Moon is in night, and the Moon makes no light. Three sunlight choices, all similar in length, so the key does not stand out. Applies the T1 bending of light to a new case.

52479c8328.why: Old tell fixed: two lures now say 'that many times', so the key is no longer the only choice tied to the stem's 400; the fourth lure is live (at new moon the Moon sits beside the Sun in the sky). The key is now the shortest choice, a weak cue that does not override the knowledge needed. Key true (NASA: the Sun is 'about 400 times bigger than the Moon' and 'about 400 times farther away'; Wikipedia, diameter and distance both about 400 times). Lures false: the umbra narrows (NASA), the air does not magnify the Moon, the Moon stays in its orbit round Earth. Old uncertain number fixed: 'rarely more than a few hundred kilometres wide' fits Wikipedia (typically 100-160 km, up to 267 km) and NASA (a typical path 'may be less than 50 miles wide'). Standard 6th-grade reason.
